fp.fragment: first-class functions, closures, iterators, generators, itertools/functools; mutation still allowed
fp.why: Jobs use callbacks, pipelines, and map/filter style without a purity checker.
fp.useWhen: When composition beats a loop and the runtime allows it.
fp.price: Not a purity guarantee; side effects remain first-class too.

sources.quote: Python programs written in functional style usually won't go to the extreme of avoiding all I/O or all assignments
Python's design offers some support for functional programming in the " Lisp tradition".

oop.fragment: class/instance model with multiple inheritance; classes are runtime objects
oop.why: Industry codebases in this family are class-shaped.
oop.useWhen: Domain models, frameworks, and types created at runtime.
oop.price: Aliasing and inheritance graphs; everything is still an object identity.

sources.quote: Python classes provide all the standard features of Object Oriented Programming: the class inheritance mechanism allows multiple base classes
Python supports multiple programming paradigms but with an emphasis on object-oriented programming and dynamic typing.

decl.reason: Python is multi-paradigm with an imperative/OO core; declaration is libraries (SQL, ORMs), not the language.

sources.quote: Most programming languages are procedural: programs are lists of instructions that tell the computer what to do with the program's input.
Multi-paradigm: object-oriented, procedural (imperative), functional, structured, reflective

actor.reason: No language-level actors/mailboxes; concurrency is threads, processes, or asyncio tasks.

sources.quote: The threading module provides a way to run multiple threads(smaller units of a process) concurrently within a single process.
Concurrency and parallelism: Multiple tasks can be run simultaneously. Python contains modules such as multiprocessing to support this form of parallelism.

static.fragment: dynamic runtime; optional erased annotations checked by external tools
static.why: Catching errors before or during running is a product bet.
static.useWhen: Match the checker to the job; the VM still runs unannotated code.
static.price: Annotations are not the runtime type system.

sources.quote: The Python runtime does not enforce function and variable type annotations. They can be used by third party tools such as type checkers, IDEs, linters, etc.
a PEP 484 “int” corresponds to Python 3's int type, which does not necessarily fits inside one machine word

strong.fragment: strong-dynamic: objects carry types; poorly defined mixed operations fail rather than coerce silently
strong.why: Coercions are where bugs hide; Python refuses many mixed-type ops.
strong.price: Duck typing still fails at use time, not definition time.

sources.quote: Despite being dynamically typed, Python is strongly typed, forbidding operations that are poorly defined
The Python runtime does not enforce function and variable type annotations.

hm.reason: Optional gradual annotations and third-party checkers; not Hindley–Milner inference in the language.

sources.quote: The Python runtime does not enforce function and variable type annotations. They can be used by third party tools such as type checkers, IDEs, linters, etc.
Python supports optional type annotations. These annotations are not enforced by the language, but may be used by external tools such as mypy

dep.reason: No Π/Σ dependent types; annotations mention types, not values as types.

sources.quote: This module provides runtime support for type hints.
Python includes a module typing including several type names for type annotations.

gen.fragment: typing.Generic / list[T] style parameters; erased at runtime
gen.why: Reuse collections and APIs across representations in checkers.
gen.price: The VM does not reify most parameters.

sources.quote: While type hints can be simple classes like float or str, they can also be more complex. The typing module provides a vocabulary of more advanced type hints.
Python includes a module`typing` including several type names for type annotations.

malloc.reason: Authors do not malloc/free ordinary objects; the implementation manages the heap.

sources.quote: Objects are never explicitly destroyed; however, when they become unreachable they may be garbage-collected.
Incminimark first allocates objects in so called nursery - place for young objects, where allocation is very cheap, being just a pointer bump.

gc.fragment: CPython: refcount plus optional cyclic GC; PyPy: incremental generational moving collector
gc.why: Throughput and safety beat explicit free for this runtime.
gc.price: CPython cycles need the collector; PyPy pauses are tracing, not refcount.

sources.quote: Since the collector supplements the reference counting already used in Python, you can disable the collector if you are sure your program does not create reference cycles.
PyPy's default garbage collector is called incminimark - it's an incremental, generational moving collector.

trace.fragment: CPython cyclic collector is generational mark-style; PyPy incminimark is tracing/moving
trace.why: Short-lived graphs and cycles the refcount cannot break.
trace.useWhen: The cycle/major collector, not the primary CPython decref path.
trace.price: CPython tracing is supplementary; PyPy tracing is the heap.

sources.quote: The GC classifies objects into three generations depending on how many collection sweeps they have survived.
Since Incminimark is an incremental GC, the major collection is incremental: the goal is not to have any pause longer than 1ms

rc.fragment: CPython primary heap is reference counting; PyPy tracing GC is not RC-primary
rc.why: Deterministic-enough destruction on CPython when counts hit zero.
rc.price: Cycles; PyPy does not share CPython's RC story.

sources.quote: CPython currently uses a reference-counting scheme with (optional) delayed detection of cyclically linked garbage
CPython has additionally the problem (1) of reference counting. With PyPy, this sub-problem is simpler: we need to make our GC multithread-aware.

own.reason: Names alias freely; no borrow checker. Multiple names bind to one object.

sources.quote: Objects have individuality, and multiple names (in multiple scopes) can be bound to the same object. This is known as aliasing in other languages.
The assignment statement (`=`) binds a name as a reference to a separate, dynamically allocated object.

thr.fragment: OS threads share memory; CPython/PyPy GIL serialises bytecode unless a free-threaded build
thr.why: Multi-core exists; this is how this language exposes shared-memory threads.
thr.useWhen: I/O-bound work or free-threaded builds; otherwise prefer processes for CPU.
thr.price: GIL, data races in extensions, or free-threaded still-opt-in.

sources.quote: CPython implementation detail: In CPython, due to the Global Interpreter Lock, only one thread can execute Python code at once
Yes, PyPy has a GIL. Removing the GIL is very hard.

coro.fragment: async/await coroutines scheduled on an event loop; PyPy also ships greenlets/stackless
coro.why: I/O without a thread per request.
coro.useWhen: Network and idle work on asyncio.
coro.price: Coloured functions; blocking the loop stalls the world.

sources.quote: Coroutines declared with the async/await syntax is the preferred way of writing asyncio applications.
Support for Stackless and greenlets are now integrated in the normal PyPy.

csp.reason: stdlib Queue is a thread-safe queue, not CSP channels in the language.

sources.quote: queue provides a thread-safe interface for exchanging data between running threads.
Python contains modules such as `multiprocessing` to support this form of parallelism.

loop.fragment: asyncio event loop runs tasks, callbacks, and I/O
loop.why: UI/network multiplexing without one thread per wait.
loop.price: One blocked turn freezes that loop.

sources.quote: The event loop is the core of every asyncio application. Event loops run asynchronous tasks and callbacks, perform network IO operations, and run subprocesses.
PyPy implements Python 2.7 and Python 3.11. It supports all of the core language. It supports the Python standard library modules.
